The naming habit is the descriptive family in its purest form: 181 names for 5,111 words, every name a full clause with its verb and its object kept, e.g. "reads the urban share as modernization" and "ties a lower death rate to higher medical development", so no name is a fragment and none is unresolved. The cost is the opposite of the 2123945 paper: the list is close to a sentence list, 181 blocks for 262 sentences, so a reader who only had the list would know what every sentence does and would still have to read the paper to find the numbers. Indicator paragraphs repeat one shape - define the indicator, then a mechanism chain, then a direction sentence - which is why the block list runs define, mechanism, mechanism, interpret four times over, and why mechanism reaches 52 blocks. Section 4 then reuses the same fifteen indicators in a bullet list twice, once for state funding and once for private funding, so fifty-two of the mechanism blocks sit in mirrored pairs and compare appears only three times, on the sentences where the private case is explicitly set against the state case.

note: Read pages 6-22 (37,920 characters) end to end. Eighteenth coarse span in the harmless direction: pages 6 to 22 open on Figure 2, one line above the section 6 heading, and carry the whole Theil model (6.1 to 6.3.4), the oligopoly and Shapley chapters 7.1 to 7.5, the path-analysis and scenario chapter 8.1 to 8.2.3, and the opening of chapter 9, so the span holds three numbered chapters and never touches the paper's policy half. Naming is the descriptive family again, 135 names for 4,258 words and 152 sentences, so nearly one name per sentence, and all 135 resolve. What the paper does is worth recording because it is a different move from the index builders: it takes a published inequality index and re-points its object. Equity is quoted from the New Palgrave as the absence of envy, and the Theil index is then extended from persons to countries by replacing income with composite national power, with the naive extension rejected by a counterexample (the United States and the Vatican would have to be power-equal) and repaired twice - a population-size weight, then a logarithmic transformation - so three derive blocks carry the whole model. Comprehensive power is then a factor analysis over twelve variables, residuals dropped on the strength of the correlations, m = 3 factors passing eighty percent, and the composite score substituted for income. The rest of the chapter is scenario arithmetic on one index: four grade sets, a mineral named Lucky that lifts a mining country's GDP by 15%, a second mineral Lucky2 that makes the payout rule explicit, a third Lucky3 that lifts every indicator by 0.05, and the same Theil plot redrawn after each: within-group curves fluctuate, the capable-versus-incapable curve jumps, and a Shapley allocation at 0.6437 and 0.5982 makes every curve fall. That is why define is thirty-two, interpret twenty-eight and read-figure twelve - the paper builds one index and then reads it back five times.

Twentieth coarse span, and it is wrong at the top end: pages 6 to 21 open inside the assumptions list, on Assumption 2 and its justification, so the first four assumptions of the paper sit above the span and only Assumptions 2 to 5 are inside it; the span then carries section 3 Model I (the capability approach, individual welfare, the three factors, the twenty-five indicators, EWM weights, GDI and the peace index, and the coefficient-of-variation equity measure with its validation), all of section 4 Model II (the GE matrix, the three asteroid types, cost, mass, time, NPV, the ME-MI investment model, the Cournot oligopoly and the 2011UW-158 example), all of section 5 on how the model changes when the throughput factor or the number of mining countries changes, and the first lines of section 6 on policy - so one span holds three numbered chapters, one of them a second model, plus the opening of the policy chapter. Naming is the descriptive family, 117 names for 4,303 words and 257 sentences, so one name per two sentences, and all 117 resolve; one of them records a printed figure-number error without losing its block, "splits countries into those needing investment and those funding themselves", which the paper attributes to Figure 6 but prints in the Figure 10 discussion. What the chapter is worth recording for is the equity measure: this is the only model in the sample that measures inequity with a coefficient of variation rather than a ratio or a distance. Each country gets an asset index and an achievement index from the same EWM pipeline, EI is their synthesis, and global equity is CV = sigma/mean over all countries, so every result in the paper is one number moving - 1.2437 and 0.5766 in 2000, 1.5332 and 0.6912 in 2020, 1.5379 and 0.6945 after one mining operation, 1.5383 and 0.6946 when the throughput factor quadruples, 1.5359 when the third level of countries joins - and the verdict is always the same sentence shape, the coefficient rose so the gap widened. That is why define is thirty-five blocks, compute fourteen and mechanism thirteen, with interpret only twelve, and why the sensitivity chapter is arithmetic on the same two numbers rather than a re-derivation.

note: Read pages 7-21 (36,110 characters) end to end. Twenty-first coarse span: pages 7 to 21 open on Table 2, the data sources, and 2.3.2 Data Filling, so the span begins one subsection above the model chapter; it then carries all of section 3 (the D&E model: four requirements, twelve inferior indicators in three dimensions, the two-layer EWM and coefficient-of-variation weighting, the Mahalanobis-distance equity score), all of section 4 (who mines, the AMO redistribution design and the P&A model), all of section 5 (the fund-pool and participation variants) and the opening of section 6 on policy - four numbered sections, and the names put no block on the data-filling bullets that open it. Naming is the descriptive family, 92 names for 4,329 words and 214 sentences, so one name per two and a half sentences, and all 92 resolve. Two things are worth copying. The first is the two-layer weighting: EWM weights the twelve inferior indicators inside each dimension and a coefficient-of-variation weighting sets the three dimension weights, so the index is built twice with no judgement asked at either level. The second is that equity is read as a distance, not a ratio: each country is a point (EMDI, TDI, EGDI), the Mahalanobis distance to the centre is summarised in a score with a mean, a maximum and a spread term, and GEI = 1000 over that score, so the paper can report 66.80 before mining and 74.67 after fifty years and speak of a 27-year recovery. Its weakness is visible in the same construction: the redistribution is the model's own invention, so the result that mining raises equity in the long run is a result about the AMO design rather than about asteroid mining, and the paper says so only indirectly when it tests the fund-pool size in section 5.1.

Four subsections pass with no block at all - 3.1.1 to 3.1.4 define social, energy, technology and economic equity in one paragraph each and none is named; 3.3 Data Preprocessing names neither the three missing-value methods nor the cost-benefit-moderate normalisation; and the entropy, coefficient-of-variation, K-means, comparative-advantage and grey-model derivations carry no name between them, because each is introduced by a name at the top of its subsection (4, 5, 7, 12) and then runs to the formula. So the two F extremes are one design decision seen twice: how finely the paper cuts its paragraphs, and whether a formula paragraph earns a block of its own. Four route blocks open sections rather than sentences (5, 10, 12, 17), which is the chapter's dominant habit; the two source blocks are the only citations the chapter makes in its own voice (2, 7), and the TOPSIS block names its authors and decade and nothing else. The equity argument is thin where it matters: fifteen of the twenty-one blocks are define, interpret, route or source, and the whole model chapter contains one compute block, one compare block, one select block and one read-figure block.

note: Read pages 5-19 (56,321 characters) end to end. Twenty-third coarse span: it opens at the 3 Model Preparation heading, so the notation table and the data-collection and data-filling pages sit above the model, and it closes inside 7.2.2, so sections 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 - the preparation, the equity model, the asteroid partial equilibrium, the impact chapter and the optimisation landscape - all count as one model chapter, five numbered sections in fifteen pages. The naming is the sixth habit and the one no reader would guess: every name is the sentence's grammatical skeleton with its content left as a placeholder - "we-observe-when-same must-both-equal-1", "goodness-of-fit close-to-1 therefore-fitting-good", "we-calculate-T=N coefficient-become much-lower", "select-N-common-factors eigenvalue-greater" - so the list locates blocks exactly, nothing is unresolved, and it says what shape each sentence has rather than what the block does. That is why the coding has to be done from the page: the same skeleton can be a check (10, the limiting case where equal RE and OE force both to one), a compute block (18, T=50 giving GE=0.4521) or a select block (22, four eigenvalues above one), and the placeholders hide every number the paper actually prints - R-squared 0.8957, Rand index 0.85, Bartlett 234.01, cumulative contribution 62.545 percent, GE 0.4521. The chapter's real weakness under this taxonomy is that it derives nothing: there is not one derive block in five sections, although the pages print the benefit-cost-interval normalisation, the entropy chain, the four chain-growth ratios and the T dataset, the exponential smoothing of dataset 2, the y = x^a fit, the integral that defines GE, the Ward sum of squares and the Rand index, the factor loading matrix and the Cobb-Douglas production function. The chapter is coded instead as five checks, five routes, four definitions and three sources, which is what the names lead a coder to do: they open subsections and report fit statistics, and the algebra between the openings goes unlabelled.

Twenty-sixth coarse span: it opens inside the assumption list, one sentence into a bullet on technology diffusion, so the glossary and the assumptions carry no block above it, and it closes inside 6.3 on policy recommendations, so sections 3 to 6 - the GGDP accounting, the fuzzy climate evaluation, the spatial game and the time-dimension carrying capacity, and the Australia case with its PVAR - pass as one model chapter, and the policy bullets at the foot belong to no block. This is the only chapter in the ledger whose names include a section title: block 6 is "It's time to make the right choice", which is the heading of task 3 printed as a name, so a name here marks a task boundary rather than a paragraph. Naming is the template family again, 21 names for roughly 5,400 words, and it is unusually rhetorical for a model chapter - five of the twenty-one blocks are world-setting rather than model-building (3 and 4 on why temperature and pollution matter, 6 as the call to decide, 13 as the hinge into the time dimension, 7 as the summary that says equity and the short run will decide), which is what an MCM task structure produces: each task needs a paragraph that motivates it before it can be answered. The first is the conversion of a policy into a growth-rate adjustment: the GGDP standard is assumed to cut the growth of Eco2, Waste and NRR by a policy factor theta = 3%, that 3% is calibrated off two events (the 2007-2008 crisis and the 2014 Sino-US statement), and every later result inherits it, so the chapter's whole forecast rests on one number that appears in a sentence and not in an equation. The second is the game's unusual payoff: the supporting countries pay a subsidy S = Rs * p, the opposing countries' payoff carries P - deltaCr + Rs * p, and the result table shows Iran accepting only in year 15 while Saudi Arabia accepts in year 13, Russia in year 10 and Australia in year 6, so the paper answers 'when' rather than 'whether' - a resolution that is passed late, country by country, is the shape of the answer.

note: Read pages 6-20 (43,596 characters of body, 5,645 words, 197 sentences) end to end. Twenty-seventh coarse span, and the first in a while whose opening is clean: it starts on the section 4 heading itself, so nothing above is orphaned. It is the tail that is cut - the span stops mid-sentence in 7.3, on "On the other hand, the economic situation of Brunei itself is", so the exhaustion arithmetic is named and its consequence, the collapse the paper goes on to model, belongs to no block. Twenty names for 5,645 words is one name per 282 words, which puts this paper beside P-F-2022-2218577 at the sparse end of the range rather than beside the sentence-list papers. What the names attach to is the rhetorical turn, not the model: three of the twenty are colon-labels ("three-category survey:", "EWM weight rationale:", "costs-discussion headed:") and seven are the paper's own sentence openers printed as names ("from-figures-observe", "seems-to-indicate", "it-can-be-foreseen", "no-one-knows then we-all-know", "it-is-worth-noting", "of-course-different", "in-any-case fortunately"), the third of the six naming habits, at its purest here. One name is a new kind and worth recording as a seventh habit: block 11 is "a bold topic heading (Intergenerational Equity), then a paragraph that unpacks the dilemma", a typesetting instruction rather than a sentence, so it names the shape of the page and none of the paper's words can be recovered from it. The cost of this naming is visible: the 21-indicator table, the four normalisation formulas, the three EWM steps, Table 3's five regressions, the GGDP rewrite and the ARIMA / GM(1,1) / SVM comparison all pass unnamed, so the chapter's whole computation chain has no name on it, and the coded mix has no derive block at all although the chapter prints a dozen formulas. Three moves are worth keeping. The first is a single scalar carrying the paper: percentDIF = |GDP - GGDP| / GDP is defined once at 4.3, and the same number then appears in the Table 3 regressions, in the ln(-%DIF) trend, in the forecast equations and in the climate rescoring, so one ratio holds the three sections together. The second is naming the payback year: the year the reformed curve overtakes the unreformed one is called the Intersection, it is forecast per country from the resource dependence rate, and Figure 10 reports it per country instead of reporting one world number, which turns a global claim into a map. The third is the three-forecaster arbitration: ARIMA and GM(1,1) are run, ARIMA is rejected because it turns the score negative in 2038 and GM(1,1) because it runs negative in 2080, SVM because it is flat, and the range is then fixed by logistic normalisation with x0 set to the median - a check that rejects models for being implausible rather than for fitting badly, and the case study is chosen the same way, Brunei because it is the extreme (60% of GDP and 90% of exports from oil and gas, GGDP per capita outside the top 100) rather than because it is typical. Section headings alliterate on M - Method, Model, Mould, Movement - which is an F-level surface trick, cheap to copy and visible on every page.

note: Read pages 5-19 (38,022 characters of body, 5,208 words, 178 sentences) end to end. Twenty-eighth coarse span and wrong at both ends again: it opens on the notation table of section 3, so the symbol list and the data description of section 4 - the six databases, the World Bank and OECD links - carry no block at all, and it closes mid-sentence in 8.3, inside the description of the EPS model, so the policy simulation the paper was building toward is never named. Eighteen names for 5,208 words is one name per 289 words, sparser still than P-F-2023-2311517 at 282 and P-F-2022-2218577 at 262. The naming family is the third habit with a label glued on: every name is a hyphenated key, a colon, and then the paper's own first clause - "two-perspectives survey:", "more-established choice:", "no-perfect-standard then simpler:", "figure-three-conclusions:" - so the list is readable at a glance and still tells the coder nothing about the job, which had to be taken from the page in every one of the eighteen cases. Three moves are worth taking. The first is the mediator: a single Climate Index is inserted between the economy and the climate, CI is regressed on GGDP with R-squared 0.987, the policy is simulated by substituting GGDP for GDP from 2000, and the finding is the difference between the two delta-CI paths read as a scalar phi - 31.57% slower deterioration on average, 5.23% during the subprime and COVID years - so a qualitative question ('does the measure help') is answered by one number with a stated sign convention and one honest exception. The second is monetising that index, which is the step that makes the cost-benefit chapter possible at all: PU in dollars is the same delta-CI difference divided by the regression slope and shifted by the intercept, so any non-monetary index in a paper can be priced by the coefficient that links it to money, and the downside is PD = delta-GDP minus delta-GDP-prime plus a correction term. The third is that correction term, and it is the most inventive and the weakest link at once: multilateral resistance is borrowed from gravity-trade work, the paper clusters 178 countries by GGDP per capita against the rate of climate deterioration, reads the four colour groups as four attitudes (green endorses, orange accepts, red resists, blue follows), and then prices resistance as Pt = k * sum of the distances the red countries must travel out of the red region, with k and b never estimated - so 'the upside is smaller than the downside for almost every year' is a sign, not a magnitude, and the chapter's verdict rests on an unexplained constant. Two smaller things to copy: the sector ratio ECRi = ECi / (NRDC + EDC) turns the national accounting identity into a per-sector share, which is how the paper gets to four sectors carrying 89.2% of environmental cost, and the ten-year plan prints three dated targets (18% off CO2 intensity by 2030, green manufacturing output, 72% off carbon intensity by 2050) that give the policy chapter something checkable. One slip is worth recording because it decides a block: the cluster discussion says 'as shown in Figure 7' but the cluster figure is Figure 8, and the ten-year target printed as 11 trillion RMB in the text is printed as $11 trillion in the schedule figure.

note: Read pages 7-18 (27,885 characters of body, 3,166 words, 117 sentences) end to end. Twenty-ninth coarse span, clean at the top and cut at the tail: it starts on the section 3 heading (Task1) and stops after Figure 12 in 6.2, so the impact section's own conclusion carries no block. Fifteen names for 3,166 words is one per 211 words, the densest of the last four but still a task-level rather than paragraph-level list: one name per task section, or two. The naming family is the 2315018 habit again - a hyphenated key, a colon, then the paper's own clause - with the content replaced by bracketed placeholders ("[N] former projects", "[area] draws large amounts", "[client] from two aspects"), so it is the template family and the label family at once and nothing in it can be turned into a job without the page. The page is a grant proposal rather than a model chapter, and that is what is worth keeping: four task sections answer four questions with documents, not with equations - 3.1 maps 764 former projects and names SEA the trending area, 3.2 draws the IWT value chain, runs results-based management and the logic framework into a problem tree, an objective tree, a logframe matrix and a Gantt chart, 4 ranks seven specialised IOs on a three-level indicator system and picks WWF at 78.70, and only then does the chapter produce algebra. Two devices from the ranking half are worth copying. The first is that the index does the choosing and the paper says so: scores from 15.81 to 78.70, the highest one executes the project, and the three indicator families are explained in one line each (organisational, communication, special influence) so the reader can see why WWF wins before seeing the number. The second is that the client is then argued to, not merely chosen: a UN Comtrade flow map establishes that SEA is the core, and a grey relational analysis over UNODC trafficking series establishes that tigers rank first at 0.83 against live reptiles 0.80 and pangolins 0.68, so the proposal's target is defended by two rankings of existing data - a cheap and honest substitute for a model that cannot be built. The one real model is the cooperation section: an expected utility with legal and illegal income, a penalty cost, a detection rate r, a Lagrange function and four comparative statics, from which 'raising r lowers the illegal share' is the whole result, and the argument that Interpol brings force while WWF brings expertise is what makes r rise. Its weakness is stated in the same place it is used: the sign of the comparative static is asserted from the signs of the derivatives (numerator negative, denominator positive) and the closed forms never appear. The impact model is OLS turned ridge: four explanatory variables and VIFs of 15.069, 13.08, 15.908 and 4.43, the switch to ridge, a trace that fixes the parameter at 0.022, and a final R-squared of 0.991 with F = 54.485 - all on n = 7 by year, which the paper reports and does not discuss, and which is the honest limit of a seven-year series with four regressors. One corpus fact has to be recorded because it decides how this chapter can be reused: the extraction has lost the algebra. All six EWM equations, the utility function, the FOCs and the ridge equations print as empty parentheses in the text, and the page also carries stray non-English watermark characters, so the names are the only reliable locator for the blocks and any clone has to take the formulas from the rendered page.

Thirtieth coarse span, wrong at both ends: page 6 opens inside the data-completion bullet list that sits above the model chapter (kindred complement, fitting complement), so the missing-value machinery carries no block, and the span stops mid-sentence in 5.6, inside the sensitivity figures. Fourteen names for 7,675 words is one per 548 words, against 289 in the sparsest of the last three, so this list is pitched at the subsection rather than the paragraph and is the coarsest read in this run. The family is the 2024 habit seen in the last three papers: a hyphenated key, a colon, then the clause, with the numbers replaced by placeholders ("[vector]", "[N]%", "$[N] billion"), so again no name yields a job. What the page shows is worth taking because the chapter's spine is unusual. It evaluates clients on a triangle of power, resources and interests, weights six indicators per corner by EWM, draws each candidate as a radar triangle, and then ranks the three categories by AHP - enterprises 1.822, governments 1.646, NGOs 0.5022 - so the choice of an enterprise client is made by an index and confirmed by a second method. The genuinely novel device is in section 4: instead of choosing a single client, the paper computes the client's complement, the vector of what LVMH lacks (0.56, 0.06, 0.76), and then searches every other profiled client by cosine similarity for the one whose strengths point in exactly that direction, landing on the government of Seychelles at 99.9% with the vector (0.35, 0.03, 0.46). That is a partner-selection rule a reader can lift whole: define the gap, then match the gap rather than the client. The profit argument is the cheap second half of the same idea - Apple's iPhone revenue of 2.01e10 times the 4.7% leather share as the cost, the mean of three comparable R&D budgets at 4.310e9 as the investment, industry sales forecasts for the return, and then an affine mapping to LVMH at 128.06e9 - which is a proportional-scaling argument the paper names honestly as roughly proportional. Three things in the results half are worth recording against it. First, the regression runs five trade categories on eight years with R-squared 0.979 and VIFs from 4.65 to 14.175, and unlike the same year's 2409949 paper this one lists the collinearity and does nothing about it. Second, the one arithmetic check a reader can run fails: 25.6 billion falling to 17.54 billion is a 31.5% fall, and the paper prints 33.81%, so the sentence that claims the target was met does not follow from its own two numbers. Third, in the five-point estimation the deviation q is printed as 2 where (5 - 4) / 0.667 gives 1.5, and the 97.3% and 87.2% that follow are not reproducible from the formulas as printed. The block list is too coarse to have caught any of these, which is the cost of one name per subsection.

The device worth taking is the use of a canonical dynamic model as an evaluation instrument: poachers are the prey and the conservation organisation the predator, and the three Lotka-Volterra coefficients are then read as organisational capabilities - PUR is the predation rate (chance of encounter times enforcement efficiency), SR the conversion rate (public support times political support), PER the reciprocal of predator mortality (funding and attention). Once the coefficients are capabilities the paper can weight them by AHP (0.43, 0.35, 0.22), score candidates on them, and choose INO at 0.51 against GA 0.42 and PAP 0.37 through CAI = (1 + IN)(CI * SC), which is a way of making a capability argument arithmetic without inventing an index. The rest of the chapter is a chain of standard pieces wired to that choice: a BP network trained on 248 records for 736 iterations, a TSP over 166 countries solved by simulated annealing, a greedy selection of five monitoring countries at a 1,000 km radius, and a heat map that reports a 23.5% fall in trade. Two things in that chain are worth recording because a writer would repeat them. First, the TSP answer is 1,696 days for one global publicity cycle, which is four and a half years of a five-year plan spent travelling, and the paper reports the number without noticing what it does to the schedule. Second, the reporting defects are the kind that survive into a submitted paper: the four R values are printed as 0.997, 0.939, 0.929 and 0.923 with the fourth labelled training for the second time, the paragraph comparing PUR and SR across the three candidates is printed twice verbatim, and the impediment model puts a Poisson lambda of 30 on bad-weather days without saying what the 30 counts. The block list at fifteen names cannot see any of this, and the one name that does name a check - 'these four R values are very close to 1' - is the check that passes.

Thirty-second F chapter, ten names for 3,078 words, one per 308 words, and the coarsest list in the ledger so far. The naming family is new in kind: the key names a rhetorical move rather than a topic - micro-motivation, cost-decomposition, revenue-simplification, functional-result, macro-extension, government-goal decomposition, GDP-expenditure decomposition, eradication-claim, short-term-framing, percentage-result table - then a colon, then a clause with the content slots replaced by placeholders. Two consequences follow and both are recordable. First, several names keep no content at all: 'it can be observed that the higher the [variable], the lower the [outcome]' is a template that would fit any paper in the corpus, and 'percentage-result table' names an artifact, not a sentence. Second, the first name is cut mid-word in storage ('net revenue from [lega') and the sentence it was taken from opens 'The conditions driving IWT behaviors were, in fact, when...', so the span opens one clause late. The span is also wrong at the top and at the tail: page 10 is the notation table and Figure 2, both unnamed, and the tail stops after the Table 2 reading, leaving the closing 'More importantly...' paragraph and section 6 unnamed - unlike the last five papers this one stops at a paragraph boundary rather than mid-sentence. The architectural device is worth taking whole: the chapter builds a micro model and then reuses it at macro level with one bridge sentence - after obtaining the micro-level model we have the ability to discuss the macro-level effects generated by the superposition of micro effects - and every qualitative goal is then forced into a normalised weighted sum, government goal as a1 GIWT + a2 GGDP + a3 Gequ with the weights summing to 1, GDP growth as wc dC + wi dI + wg dG with weights summing to 1, so the policy question becomes one scalar maximisation over one decision variable, the split between infrastructure and agricultural subsidy. Two smaller moves travel well. Distributive equity is measured as a ratio of the two wage changes rather than a level, so it needs no distributional data. And the budget constraint is anchored to last year's growth, Bt = Bt-1 + rho(dInfra + dSub), which makes the programme self-financing and turns rho into the actual ask. Against that, three things a reader can check do not hold. Eq 11 prints ti = max{0, -53 wi + 20}, so any hourly wage above 20/53 = 0.38 dollars drives the model answer to zero, which means the calibration predicts that nobody in Tanzania poaches, and the paper then justifies a sixteen-year eradication path with that model. The constants 53 and 20 appear nowhere with a substitution table, so the closed form cannot be reproduced from Table 1. And three horizons are used without ever being reconciled - sixteen years to eradicate, a thirty-year optimisation cycle, five years of short-term effects - each section choosing its own. Corpus defect to record: the Table 1 notation block is interleaved by the CHIP and MATHmodels watermarks so symbols, descriptions and values are misaligned row by row, and a clone must rebuild that table from the render.

Thirty-fourth F chapter and the first 2025 paper in the run, so the naming family changes completely: these names do not describe a block's content at all, they label a sentence pattern and quote its opener - 'Model selection justification chain: "The reason for choosing...is mainly based on" followed by enum', 'Advantage enumeration with transitions: "First...Secondly...In addition...Finally"', 'Summary sentence with conditional reasoning: "In summary, given the...it is reasonable to choose"', 'Finding-bullet pattern with "characterized by"'. That is the eighth naming habit, after fragments, the printing-error note, the sentence-opener, the descriptive list, the opening-only list, the placeholder template and the layout instruction, and it is the one that makes coding hardest, because a name of this kind can only be matched if the reader recognises the pattern in the pages. The names are also one per sentence rather than one per block: three consecutive names (selection chain, advantage enumeration, summary sentence) all describe the same justification paragraph for the variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, so a paragraph of 250 words carries three blocks. Eight names over four pages of which five are selection moves, because this declared model chapter is almost entirely method justification - PCA for 136 and 825 indicators down to 8 and 12 dimensions at 90% explained variance, then VBGMM, then the two-level unordered multinomial logistic regression. Extraction is the worst in the ledger so far and has to be recorded before anything else: 665 of the 2,208 tokens in the span, thirty per cent, are the m-runs left where Figures 4 and 5 were, so the prose the names describe is about 1,543 words and the density is one name per 193 words of real text rather than one per 276. The span is also wrong at both ends: page 7 opens at 5.2, so section 5.1 and whatever precedes it carry no name, and the tail stops inside the fourth finding bullet at 'This can greatly increase the possibility of bringing criminals to justice'. One layout defect inside the span is worth recording because it is the kind that survives review: Table 2, an EM algorithm for censored survival data, is printed in the middle of 5.2.2 between the VBGMM text and Figure 4, with no sentence anywhere referring to it, so a clustering section carries a survival-analysis table from another part of the paper. On what the chapter shows: the two-level structure is a clean template - level one regresses the outcome on case-level factors, level two regresses the level-one intercepts on country-level factors, and the paper writes both out as explicit equations, three log-odds equations for four outcome categories at layer one and three intercept equations on five Z indices borrowed from the GCI index at layer two - so the whole country-level story is carried by five numbers per outcome rather than a second model. Three checks a reader can run on it. The collinearity pre-check is asserted and not shown: the sentence says the variance inflation factor is below 10 'within a reasonable range' with no table and no values. No fit statistic appears anywhere in the span - no log-likelihood, no AIC, no sample size, no p values - so none of the twelve printed coefficients can be falsified. And the coefficients themselves are on a raw scale: -16.351 and 11.218 on log-odds are odds ratios of 1e-7 and 7e4, which means the predictors were never standardised and the layers are not comparable, while the finding bullets then read the signs in words: the success bullet says 'fewer assets exposed to potential attackers' although the X2 term in the success equation is the only positive one printed, so either X2 is coded as exposure rather than security or the prose reverses the sign, and the paper never says which.

note: Read pages 7-16 (40,247 characters of extraction, 3,814 tokens, 118 sentences) end to end. Thirty-fifth F chapter and the second 2025 paper, thirteen names for 3,814 tokens, one per 293, or one per 191 of the 2,485 real words once the 1,329 m-tokens are removed - thirty-five per cent of the span is figure noise left by the watermark. The naming family is a third kind in two papers: the 2025 habit is the imperative instruction. Every name here is a verb-first order to the writer with no subject and no content - 'Introduce selected algorithm with core principle', 'State objective function in plain language before formula', 'Reference prior claim to justify hyperparameter selection method', 'Transition from clustering results to next model by claiming factor identification', 'Motivate custom formulation by citing domain-specific structure' - so the list reads as annotation guidance about how a block should be built rather than as a description of what this block does. That is the closest the corpus comes to publishing its own rubric, and it is the easiest family to confuse with the layout-instruction habit, the difference being that those describe the page and these describe the rhetoric. The span is wrong at both ends: page 7 opens mid-sentence inside the one-hot encoding of section 4.1 ('method, each categorical feature mentioned above was converted into a binary vector'), so the preprocessing that the clustering depends on carries no name, and the tail stops inside the third of the high-GCI bullets on page 16. The equations are the real loss in this chapter and a clone has to know it: the K-means objective, both Gower distance formulas, the regularised objective with its Hadamard product, the Lagrange solution, the association strength matrix, the constraint and the integer programming model all come out of the extraction as parenthetical symbol glossaries with the formulas themselves missing, so only text survives and every equation must be taken from the render. On the chapter's argument, two structural moves and two defects. The move is the layering of a data-driven half on a theory half: K-means with elbow-chosen K, chi-square screening of features, PCA for display, then a mapping of every cluster onto a Chinese Five Elements scheme whose generation and restriction relations become the model's constraints, so a clustering result is re-read as five elements with an association matrix and a mutual generation/restriction matrix of 1 and -1. That is a strong template for a paper that needs a theory spine without inventing one: cluster first, then rename the clusters. The defects are both circularities of the same kind. The elbow chooses K = 5 and the model then has exactly five elements, one cluster per element, so the data cannot disagree with the theory; and the cluster summaries are printed as bare thresholds - firewall deployment above 70%, social network attacks above 50%, DDoS above 60% - which the next section reuses verbatim as the criteria that define Metal, Wood and Fire, so a centroid becomes a theoretical category by repetition. Two more checks fail outright: the chi-square test is reported as p below 0.05 with no statistic and no table, and the risk direction flips inside the chapter, 5.3.1 asserting that low GCI scores mean higher risk while 5.3.3 reports that Russia, Ukraine and the United States 'have higher scores, indicating greater vulnerability', which reverses the index it just defined.

Thirty-sixth F chapter and the shortest list since the very coarse 2016-43181 record: six names, and after removing the 2,061 m-tokens the real prose is 1,442 words, one name per 240. This extraction is the worst in the ledger, fifty-nine per cent of its tokens being watermark noise, and the noise is not a block but a column running down every page, so the text has to be reassembled by hand before it can be read at all. The naming family continues 2025's verbless descriptive labels - 'cluster count justification with two metrics', 'topic enumeration with keyword anchors', 'DID design and group construction' - which is the same annotator voice as the previous two papers with the imperative softened into a noun phrase. The span is wrong at both ends: page 10 opens on the elbow and silhouette figure itself with no heading above it, and the tail stops at the end of the control-variable list in 5.1.2, before the DID coefficient is ever shown. What the chapter actually establishes is worth recording because it is the opposite of what the label says: this declared model chapter contains no model. There is no K-means objective, no LDA generative model and no DID regression equation anywhere in the five pages - the chapter is a design chapter, six blocks of prose describing how countries were clustered, how policy text was cleaned, how six topics were named by keywords, and how treated and control countries were matched. Zero derive, zero compute, zero read-figure across it, and the arithmetic that does appear is a figure the blocks do not read. Two checks a reader can run. The elbow series is printed plainly - inertia 248, 189, 130, 104, 85, 78, 66, 56 for K from two to nine - and the successive falls are 24, 31, 20, 18, 8, 15 and 15 per cent, so the sharpest bend is at K = 4, not the K = 3 the paper adopts; the silhouette panel may well justify three, but the elbow argument as printed does not. And the DID is run with '1-2 countries' in the treatment group and a matched set of the same size, so there is no inference to make and the paper reports no coefficient, no standard error and no specification inside the span. Two smaller things belong in the record. The treatment variable is defined as one 'if that country had implemented the relevant policy in year, while 0 means no implementation', with the year left blank in the print. And the figure captions are unspaced and mislabelled - 'Figure6', 'Figure7', 'Figure8', with an axis reading 'Nuber of culsters(K)' - so a clone cannot take caption formatting from this paper.

Second chapter in the corpus whose six stored names are the identical string 'model-establishment paragraph N: purpose -> variables -> equation -> interpretation', the first being P-F-2016-43181, so the template family is not a one-off five years back: it is still being produced in 2025. The names segment nothing, so the chapter was split by hand into eleven blocks and this record carries segmentation 'own' and stays out of every share and every pair count, exactly as the 2016 record does. Real words after removing the 2,061 m-tokens are 2,847, one hand-made block per 259. The span is wrong at both ends: page 8 opens with the Fig.4 caption and the data-filtering prose of the section above, and page 18 runs into '4. Results and Discussion' and stops there, so the declared model chapter ends inside the results. The chapter itself is worth reading because it is the most complete data-preparation record in the F sample: four index formulas for being found, thwarted, causing loss and severity, each written as a ratio over n_it with a binomial loss indicator and a denominator correction that subtracts the suspected and unrated events; a note that annual data hides mid-year policy changes so the analysis goes monthly; a remainder rule that spreads the twelve-month discrepancy by 12 and hands the leftover units out in the order 1, 4, 7, 10, 2, 5, 8, 11, 3, 6, 9, 12; six UNESCO demographic factors with a stated interpolation rule (zeros before the first non-zero value, forward fill after it); a de-duplication of the June 2023 US spike, where 735 near-identical records become 17 distinct events; three correlation coefficients computed and tabulated for six features; and a TimeXer model described entirely in prose - patches, variate-level embeddings, self-attention inside the endogenous variable, cross-attention to the exogenous ones, and learnable global tokens as the bridge. Five checks a reader can run. The de-duplication silently redefines the dependent variable for one month, replacing a count of records with a count of distinct events, and nothing in the text reconciles the two definitions. The claim that Network Server has 'the lowest correlation values, all of which are closest to 0' holds only for Pearson: for Spearman it is 0.177 for Literacy against 0.196 for Server, and for Kendall 0.162 against 0.166, so Literacy is the flattest in two of the three tables. Kendall's tau is compared with Pearson's r and Spearman's rho as if the three sat on one scale, which they do not, tau being bounded at about two-thirds of rho for monotone dependence. The paper keeps Enrollment at +0.321 while dropping Literacy at +0.249 as a data gap, and never remarks that its other education measure, public spending on education, correlates negatively at -0.289, so two education indicators point opposite ways and only one of them is discussed. And the leftover-unit order 1, 4, 7, 10, 2, 5, 8, 11, 3, 6, 9, 12 is given with no reason, so which months receive the imputed unit is arbitrary. One printing defect: the sentence introducing the spike says 'As shown in Figure M', an unreplaced placeholder in the body text rather than in a caption.

Third, the height read reports the gain reversing above roughly 15 m and then recommends building high within 3-6 m, so the branch that motivated the reading is never inside the design range, and the 15 m is glossed as 'possibly the same value of the width', a numeric coincidence offered as a mechanism. Second, the branching table has no true-value column at all - the error is the gap between the model's wind torque 0.0068 and its own gravity torque 0.0063, so the validation is the model checked against itself, and that gap is 7.4 percent, not the printed 6.53. Nine hyphenated artifact keys, the same family as the first and fifth records, five of them ending in -output, -result or -table. The span is the longest in the sample: it opens on the last seven AHP weights with no sentence above them and runs through the maple classification test, all of Model Two (leaf distribution), all of Model Three (tree profile against leaf shape), all of Model Four (leaf mass) and stops on the Strengths and Weaknesses heading - four models, and each model's own introduction, hypothesis and derivation is inside the results span, so the name list covers four chapters' worth of work with nine names. Five checks. First, and it is the interesting one, all three regressions reproduce: recomputing the least squares from the printed five pairs gives slopes 0.3906, 0.2055 and 0.6567 against printed 0.3905, 0.2055 and 0.6567, intercepts 0.3614, 0.6208 and 0.1900 exactly, r-squared 0.174, 0.798 and 0.965 against printed 0.1783, 0.7985 and 0.9645, and F of 0.63, 11.87 and 82.0 against printed 0.63, 11.8857 and 81.5595 - so this is the first chapter in the branch whose arithmetic survives being recomputed, and the defect is elsewhere. Second, the AHP weights connect to nothing: the deviation index is printed as a sum over I1 to I7, and all six category columns add up to their printed ID exactly, but a plain sum is what reproduces, so the seven weights, the lambda, the CI and the CR are computed and then never used in the classification they were built for. The consistency check also misquotes its own criterion, 'CR < 0.01' where Saaty's threshold is 0.10, and CI = (7.0512 - 7)/6 = 0.0085 against a printed 0.0087. Third, the classification is not a test: the paper says it compared the maple with the six categories and found it resembles Category 4 most, and only then runs the model to confirm, so one leaf, a hypothesis fixed by eye and no held-out case underlie the claim in 5.4 that the model classifies 'any given leaf reliably'. Fourth, the latitude test is an identity plus a typo: tan alpha = h/L is the model's own optimum rearranged, the conversion is alpha to 90 - alpha, and all three predicted latitudes reproduce exactly (38.66, 28.4, 33.69 against printed 38.65, 28.39, 33.69), which means it tests whether real trees sit at the predicted internode ratio and nothing else; the first row's true latitude is printed as '35~35', a zero-width band that excludes the predicted 38.65, so the sentence claiming every prediction falls inside its true range is false on the table's own numbers. The model's definition of alpha is also wrong astronomy - the greatest annual solar altitude is at the solstice, not at the vernal equinox, though the equinox conversion is the one actually used. Fifth, the leaf-mass table prints 360 cells and no intermediate: the CO2 column, the fit statistics for the quadratic that produced it and the units bridge are all absent, and the fit is described as 'actually fit the data perfectly' with no number, while the age-size model is printed with a sign that cannot grow, P = k1 (1 - e^{k2 A}) with positive k2 falling with age and its transform A = k4 ln(1 - k5 P^{k6}) taking the log of a bounded argument. Eight hyphenated artifact keys, the fourth record of that family. The span opens mid-sentence on 'SEtotal is [0, 1]' so the definition of the score the whole chapter ranks by is cut off above the heading, and it closes on the last paragraph of section 7, which means the authors' own improvement section, 6.1 to 6.3, is inside the results span and unnamed: three self-declared defects - leaf classification that ignores photosynthesis type, a grid algorithm that cannot tell big leaves apart, a photosynthesis model with one input - collapse into a single name together with the conclusion. What the blocks do: four leaf types scored under three tree profiles and the best one chosen per profile; the poplar figure read with the remark that when theta and phi are small the irradiance is largest; the claim that the hypothesis stands because the results are generally expected; a sample-size limit handed to the reader; a field measurement of thirty-two coordinate systems to pick the simulated tree closest to a real camphor; the mass chain LMA times leaf area; a thirty-point sweep of three crown profiles over height; four regression plots; and a closing bounded interpretation. Five checks. First, the comparison that carries the hypothesis cannot discriminate where it is used: the poplar column reads 0.62, 0.49, 0.63, 0.62, so the chosen shape wins by 0.01, the Japanese banana column reads 0.82, 0.83, 0.82, 0.85, a spread of 0.03, and section 6.2 admits in the authors' own words that for big leaves the grid algorithm 'tends to generate similar results for different leaf shapes' - the paper states the failure of its own discriminator three pages after using it to rank. Second, the verification sentence is 'since the results are generally expected, our hypothesis stands', which is confirmation by expectation rather than by test. Third, the case study transposes a digit in its own input: the average LMA is derived as 177.74 g per m2 and the mass line multiplies 177.47 by 72 m2 to 12,777.84 g, which is exact for the transposed value, so the error is in the input and not the product. Fourth, the scale bridge is a bare factor: the polygon output 150.0359 becomes 6.001436 m2, exactly a division by 25, an unstated length scale of 5, and the leaf is modelled as a rhombus with a longer diagonal of 0.25 in unspecified units against a measured transverse diameter of 5 cm, so the simulation and the tree are never tied together on the page. Fifth, the sweep is miscounted and mislabelled: three profiles at heights from 5 to 10 m in 0.5 m steps is thirty-three simulations and the text says 'the total 30 data', and the sentence says the sweep calculates total leaf area while the regression it feeds is described as leaf mass. On top of those, four regressions are reported with no coefficient, no r-squared and no p value anywhere, and the one quantitative claim made from them, that mass grows cubically with height for similar crown profiles, contradicts the paper's own geometry, since a similar profile makes ground area proportional to height squared. Two notes for reuse. The naming is the artifact-key family again but its keys are process keys rather than object keys - 'case-tree mass chain', 'height-profile sweep', 'profile-stratified regression' - which is the most informative variant of the habit in this branch, because each name says what operation the block performs and a coder can label it without reading the page. And the move worth copying is the unnamed one: section 6 lists the model's defects one by one, each tied to the section it comes from, which is a strength-and-weakness block written as an improvement list rather than as an apology.
