note: Thirtieth type-A record, and the widest span so far: file pages 4 to 14, printed 3 to 13, beginning mid-sentence inside the Introduction subsection C, Our Model, and then carrying the whole of II Background, A transmitter and receiver, B radio propagation and loss, C skywave channel interaction, D performance evaluation, the whole of III Assumptions, the Nomenclature table, all of IV Model Development, A construction with its three subsections and B validation, and it stops on the last page as V Model Application opens. Because the span carries background and assumptions, its profile of fifteen define blocks out of twenty-nine is inflated by construction and this record should be read as the paper's whole front half rather than as a model chapter. Twelve stored names, and they are the fourth naming family in this ledger: every one begins with the identical prefix, 'Use this ordered move to make Model Construction auditable:', and the only content is the four-stage arrow chain after it, so the names describe the computation rather than the topic and are more useful than any stub family before, but they also guarantee that twelve names cover twelve moves of one kind and never mark a figure, a source choice or a result. Two of the twelve do not resolve. Name 7, path-dependent electron density and collisions into non-deviative absorption, has no paragraph anywhere in the paper: the only occurrences of absorption after the background pages are the symbol k in the nomenclature table and the term L_absorption inside (22). Name 8, great-circle distance and bearing into a landing position, has no paragraph inside the span, and the bearing and position material sits on page 15 in the scenario setup and again in the memo. Both are recorded unresolved rather than guessed. Five numbers in the chapter are right and I checked each: 100 W is 50 dBm as printed; the budget is 180.06 dB deep and the remaining allowance to hold a 10 dB margin over a -120 dBm floor is 170.06, which is the printed 180 and 170; the phase dispersion 4 pi dh sin(theta)/lambda is the Rayleigh form; the complex term gamma = 18e9 sigma / f is the 60 lambda sigma imaginary part written for f in hertz, giving 30,000 for sea water at 3 MHz; and the reflection law (20) with its cosine (21) is the vector form of equal angles. Verified defects. The two loss terms the budget rests on are never written: L_free and L_absorption enter (22) and the hop count depends on them, while the only term with an equation behind it is the terrain term, so a chapter that derives a Fresnel coefficient to the third decimal leaves the free-space and absorption debits as words. The quantitative validation is a restatement of the background: pages 6 and 14 give the same 2500 to 5000 km hop range, and the second is offered as the model's result. Two scale faults on the terrain patch: the ten by ten metre mesh cannot carry the fifteen metre swell the same paper imposes as the super-turbulent sea, and the fifty by fifty sample of one-arcsecond SRTM data spans about 1.5 km, so rescaling it to ten metres compresses the horizontal scale about 151 times, which means a 45 degree facet in the model would need 1.5 km of relief in the source data. Two artefacts of bookkeeping: the NASA epoch is 1 January 2001 at 1:30 GMT on page 10 and 1 January 2000 on page 14, and the nomenclature gives A in km and B in m, two path lengths in two units in one table. And the assumption that a mountainous region has sharp deviations in the tens of metres is followed, eight pages later, by a mesh whose elevation changes are smoothed to ten metres or less. No density figure is recorded: pages 4 to 14 hold 3,855 words against 984 claimed, because the claimed count is the sum of the twelve named moves and because problem-analysis, data-preprocessing, algorithm, robustness and results spans all overlap these pages.

note: Thirty-first type-A record and the worst naming in the ledger. The fifteen stored names are three themes crossed with five rhetorical forms: screen inadmissible cases, extend a transparent baseline through a correction interface, expose shared structure while isolating the parameters that change across media, each repeated verbatim for the paragraph-chain form, the compact-sentence form, the evidence-bridge form, the handoff-transition form and the boundary-check form. Not one word of the fifteen refers to this paper, its ionosphere, its sea surface or its terrain, so the field holds a template grid rather than names; the chapter was coded from the pages and the record carries the placeholder flag. The span is file pages 6 to 16, printed 5 to 14: the tail of the assumption list, the notation table, 3.1 model description, 3.2 the ionosphere in five subsections from the D-layer attenuation through the refractive index, the E layer, the F layer with its micro-element recursion and the MUF, 3.3 the sea, 3.4 the ground, 3.5 free-space path loss and 3.6 background noise, and it stops on the noise figure as 4 Result begins. Six things in it are right and I checked each: the wavelength to frequency correspondence, 20, 17 and 15 m against 15, 17.65 and 20 MHz; the imaginary coefficient 300 lambda, which is 60 lambda sigma with sigma at 5 S/m, giving 4,500 at 15 m; the resistivity to conductivity inversion, 10 to 100 ohm metres becoming 0.01 to 0.1 siemens per metre with the midpoint 0.05 taken; the 32.45 constant of (13) for kilometres and megahertz; the critical condition that reflection begins when the ray angle reaches 90 degrees; and the choice of horizontal polarization, which is the flatter of the two coefficients against grazing angle and is shown to be so in both Figure 5 and Figure 7. Verified defects. The advice in 3.4 contradicts its own sentence: the paragraph reads the reduction factor as falling when the grazing angle rises, which makes small grazing angles the good ones, then says that electromagnetic waves with a small incident angle are the ones likely to lose energy, and then recommends the small grazing angle, so incidence and grazing are collapsed into one phrase and the middle sentence is wrong as printed. The ground is a building material: relative permittivity 15 from a range given for wet concrete and conductivity 0.05 from a range given for concrete, with no statement of what terrain the problem's ground is meant to be, so the dry-mountain case of the question is answered with a wall. The physical unit is printed with an equals sign where the division belongs, dB=km for the D-layer coefficient and m=s and 10-100 m for metres per second and ohm metres in 3.4, and the figure caption repeats it. And the span ends without a budget: the D-layer attenuation, the surface reflection, the free-space loss and the background noise are each derived in turn and nothing joins the four into a received power inside these pages. One cross-paper check rather than a defect: the imaginary part of the permittivity is printed here as 70 plus i300 lambda and in P-A-2018-76082 as 70 minus 4,500i, the same 60 lambda sigma term at 15 m, so the two cannot both match their own Fresnel forms, but the extraction drops signs in several places and I record this as a sign to check, not as arithmetic to correct. No density figure is recorded: 2,320 words on those pages against 552 claimed, with four other spans overlapping them.

note: Thirty-second type-A record. The thirty-six stored names are nine themes crossed with four rhetorical forms, the paragraph-chain, compact-sentence, evidence-handoff and boundary-check forms, so the field is a template grid again and the chapter was coded from the pages; unlike P-A-2018-77845 the nine themes are this paper's own moves, wave complexity to a computable surrogate, three-dimensional extension, geometric upper bound, dominant-loss triage, baseline then correction, correction composition, signal-noise gate, cross-medium analogy and static-model boundary, and each theme carries a page and a real source excerpt, but nine phrases still cannot name thirty-four blocks. Span is file pages 7 to 21, printed 4 to 18: the notation table, 4.1 HF propagation and the ionosphere and the usable frequency, 4.2 the Longuet-Higgins, spectral and three-dimensional wave models with the simulation figure, 4.3 the four-part budget, free-space loss and the one-jump bound, absorption with the index that is then dropped for a constant, calm and turbulent sea reflection with the two correction factors, the additional loss, the first reflection intensity, field strength, noise and SNR, the hop scaling, 5 the ground comparison, 6.1 the moving-receiver time budget, 6.2 the frequency table, and it stops inside 7 Strengths. Eight things are right and I checked each: the band correspondence, 3 to 30 MHz against 100 to 10 m; the 0.85 MUF operating point; the wind reference 19.5 m of the PM spectrum; the 234.0 that (22) builds from 137.2 plus 96.8 and then reduces to 201.56 by taking 32.44 out of the free-space term; the cancellation of 20 lg f between (20) and (21), which leaves the frequency dependence of (22) coming only from the path-loss term, 23.52 dB at 15 MHz; the one-jump bound itself, which with 6371 km, a 3 degree minimum elevation and a 300 km virtual height gives 3224.5 km, exactly the r the table uses for one hop; the hop arithmetic, 3225 doubled to 6450 printed as 6449 and tripled to 9675 printed as 9674; and the 3000 km refit step, which is that same 3225 km rounded. Verified defects. (5) prints Li while the notation table and every heading say La, so the budget names a symbol that is never defined. (19) describes P1 as the transmitting power and P0 as the first reflection intensity, which reverses both the notation table and Table 1, where P0 is the 100 W transmitter. The one-jump bound is stated as 4000 km for F2 and then contradicted by the paper's own table, which uses the 3225 km the formula actually gives, so the text and the numbers come from two different virtual heights with no reconciliation. Table 1 sets the working frequency to 100 MHz for a paper whose own band is 3 to 30 MHz, and Table 4 is headed f = 15 Hz where the text says 15 MHz. The four printed SNR rows cannot come from one set of parameters: with (22) and (23) to (25), differencing consecutive rows implies a reflection loss of about 20.8 dB between one hop and two, then minus 1.2 dB between two and three, then 2.6 dB between three and four, and the two unknowns that would absorb a constant, the noise bandwidth and the atmospheric noise figure, cancel in the differences; and 20.8 dB is impossible for this paper's own reflection model, because both correction factors are fractions and the calm coefficient cannot exceed one, so a first-hop loss that large needs a product of correction factors near 0.0083, which no figure in the paper shows. That same implied loss also contradicts the comparison in 5, where flat ground at 6.53 dB is presented as the worse surface and still reaches four hops against the sea's six. The absorption index (9) is derived from a sunspot number and a zenith angle that are never given a value, and is then replaced by a constant 4 dB, so the formula is decorative at the only place it could be used. The equation numbering is not a count: 24 is printed twice, for the hop-scaled reflection loss and again for the SNR threshold, and 26 is never printed at all. The bandwidth is labelled in dB inside a 10 lg term, the same unit error as in P-A-2018-76082. The antenna gain of (20) disappears from (22) with no statement that it is taken as unity. The six hops returned by fsolve arrive with no stated target, while (24) does state one, SNR at or above 10 dB, and by Table 4 that boundary is reached at four hops over 10,125 km, with five and six only at shorter ranges, so the six is a stopping choice and not a computed maximum. In the wave model the random initial phase is drawn between 0 and a quarter period, which biases the superposition instead of randomizing it. And the absolute level of every SNR cannot be checked at all: the noise bandwidth and the atmospheric noise figure are never printed, and Table 2 is an image of the CCIR data with no single value quoted in the text. note: Thirty-third type-A record, and the purest instruction-template naming in the ledger. The fifteen stored names are five move labels crossed with three rhetorical forms, paragraph-chain, sentence-frame and handoff-boundary, and the function body in every one of them is the same boilerplate sentence, expand the complete observable paragraph progression for the action of something while preserving some boundary, so only the slot label names anything at all; but the five slots are real landmarks, 4.1 opening, Rate closure, Equations 2-4, Figure 1 interpretation and Weight-to-energy handoff, and the chapter was coded from the pages with the record flagged. Span is file pages 5 to 7, printed 4 to 6: the notation table, 4.1 the logistic weight model from the observation that growth decelerates through (1), the initial value problem (2), its closed form (3), the three data points and the fitted (4) with Figure 1 and the reading that puts maturity at eight years, then 4.2.1 Kleiber's law, the human metabolic formula (5), the 80 kg man and the 2,751 kcal reference, the ratio (6) and the substituted curve (7), and it stops as 4.2.2 opens. Five things are right: (3) is the exact solution of (2); (5) returns 1,926 kcal a day for 80 kg, 180 cm and 20 years with the standard men's coefficients, 13.7, 5, minus 6.8 and 66; the division by 0.7 gives 2,751.4, printed as 2,751; (6) applies the three-quarter exponent to the mass ratio and not to the mass; and (4) at age three returns 14,003.8 kg, which is the 14,000 kg datum. Verified defects, and this is the worst arithmetic in the A sample. (4) does not pass through the second datum: evaluated at one year it returns 112.45 kg against the stated 35 kg, so the printed curve fits birth and age three and ignores the middle point. The three points cannot be fit by this model at all: with a birth mass of 10 kg, a logistic through 35 kg at one year and 14,000 kg at three years has no solution, and the weight at age three cannot exceed about 429 kg however large the asymptote is made, so the calibration is impossible rather than merely inaccurate. The asymptote is 1,481,000 kg, one thousand four hundred and eighty-one tonnes, against the 14 tonnes the paper calls the adult dragon, and because the figure's vertical axis is labelled in units of one hundred thousand kilograms the plot reads as a curve topping out at 14.8; the text then reads that asymptote as the dragon reaching its maximum weight at eight years and calls the animal mature there. (7) is not (6) with the paper's own reference mass: at age zero (6) forces the dragon to consume exactly 2,751 kcal a day, and (7) returns 646, so the printed constant is 4.26 times too small and is exactly what (6) gives with a reference mass near 69 kg rather than the 10 kg birth mass. (5) also reuses w0 for the man's weight, a symbol the notation table assigns to the dragon's birth mass, and introduces h0 and a0 that the table does not list. And the formula is attributed to the American Sports Medicine Association when it is the Mifflin-St Jeor equation for men. Two smaller ones: (1) prints r where the surrounding text and (2) use r0, and 4.2.2 opens by referring to the calorie consumption at one year old, which 4.2.1 never evaluates. No density figure: 1,091 words on those pages against 243 claimed, with six other spans overlapping them.

note: Thirty-fourth type-A record, the second dragon paper of 2019 and the second instruction-template naming. The eighteen stored names are six move labels crossed with three rhetorical forms, expand the progression for something, compress it to one source-bounded sentence frame, preserve the transition and terminal boundary, and each body is a fixed sentence with a variable slot, so only the slot names anything; the slots are real landmarks, Balerion scaling, the two-analogue estimate, growth data selection, model selection, the length-to-mass modification and the fitted curve, and the chapter was coded from the pages with the record flagged. Span is file and printed pages 4 to 7: 3.3 the case for indeterminate growth, 3.3.1 sizing Balerion by scaling a crocodile by its teeth and then bracketing a pterosaur against a komodo dragon, 3.3.2 the candidate growth families and the choice, 3.3.3 the von Bertalanffy form carried to weight, the parameter list, the anchors and the rejection of the problem's given weights, the episode sizes, the fitted curve, and 3.4 the metabolic rate from a human to an elephant to a blue whale with the cow count, and it stops on Balerion's daily requirement. Nine numbers are right and I checked each: one watt per kilogram as 20.65 kcal per kilogram a day, which is 86,400 joules over 4,184; 65.3 as 20.65 times the fourth root of 100; the elephant at 8.82 kcal per kilogram; the daily need as rate times mass, 65.3 times W to the three quarters; Balerion at 663,107 kcal and 1.33 cows; 979.7 kW for 40.46 cows; the whale at 8.7 kcal per kilogram and the 177.4 rebasing; 3.6 cows on the whale-based law; and the fitted curve itself, which returns 5.02 kg at birth, 29.77 kg at one year, 219,901 kg at 220 years and 2,238 kg at nine years, giving 21,249 kcal a day against the printed 21,247. Verified defects. The pterosaur estimate is a factor of ten out: 250 kg scaled by the cube of 150 over 9 is 1,157,407 kg, printed as 115,740. The komodo estimate silently uses the fifty metre length that the crocodile scaling produced, after the paragraph above has fixed Balerion at forty-two metres; at forty-two metres the same law gives 192,080 kg, and the printed 324,074 is exactly 70 times the cube of fifty over three. The average of the two printed weights is 219,907, printed as 219,901, and that figure then becomes the anchor of every fit in the paper. The model choice contradicts the requirement it states: the section argues the dragons grow without limit and so there should be no asymptote, then adopts the one equation it has just called bounded, and the resolution it offers, early exponential growth, does not remove the bound; the fitted bound is 223,348 kg, 1.6 percent above Balerion, so the chosen model's ceiling is the largest known dragon's own weight and the premise does no work. The no-limit alternative is stated with the condition that any y with a second derivative below one qualifies, which is dimensionally meaningless and is not the condition for attenuating growth. The metabolic conversion is halved: the range 0.3 to 9 watts per kilogram is written as 3 to 92 kcal per kilogram against the paper's own 20.65 kcal per watt per kilogram, so the correct range is 6.2 to 186 and the cow bracket of 1.32 to 40.46 should be about 2.7 to 83. The fitted curve is written in x where the model is parameterised in t. And the assumption that dragons live about 250 years is justified by a dragon that lived to 220 and then never used, because every fit anchors on 220. No density figure: 1,539 words on those pages against 665 claimed, with six other spans overlapping them.

The thirty-three stored names are eleven move labels crossed with three rhetorical forms, and every body is a fixed sentence around a slot, so only the slot names anything; the slots come straight from the section numbering, Section 3 opening, Figure 1, 3.1, 3.1.1, 3.1.2, Equation 2-3, Figure 2, 3.1.3, 3.2, 3.3, Equation 7-8, and the chapter was coded from the pages with the record flagged. Span is file pages 5 to 9, printed 2 to 6: the end of the assumption list, the symbol table, Section 3 and its framework figure, 3.1 energy expenditure with Kleiber's law, the rest and action split, the four flying animals, the log-linear fit and the two constants, 3.1.3 the fire-breathing mechanism and its roasting energy, 3.2 the food chain with the assimilation rate, 3.3 the energy budget with (5) to (8), and 3.4.1 opens the size bound with the bone table before the span ends on the stress formula. Four things are right and I checked each: the two constants are the exponentials of the printed intercepts, 36.6 and 270.4, and both then reproduce all eight table values to within about a fifth, with the rest line low by five percent at the smallest bird and high by eleven at the largest; the slope of minus 0.25 is exactly the b minus one of the same section, so the fit and the law agree by construction; (6) is algebraically what it claims, assimilated minus fire equals intake times a constant; and (7) and (8) differentiate (5) and (6) consistently, with the expenditure rate of (4) entering unchanged. Verified defects. Table 3 breaks its own rule: the text says the assimilation rate can be had from respiration, which makes it 60 to 70 percent, 40 to 50 and 5 to 10 for the three classes, and the table prints 60 to 70, 70 to 80 and 90 to 95, so two of its three rows contradict the method that produced the column and the dragon's 90 percent is taken from a row that cannot be derived that way. The coefficient K of (6) to (8) is the whole point of folding the fire cost into the energy budget and is never evaluated, although the paper's own two constants make it 0.5655. The fire constant 6.69 million joules per kilogram of food is labelled estimation with no calculation behind it, against an intake of 20 million joules per kilogram in the same pages, so a third of the assimilated energy goes to roasting. And the last coded page defines the stress formula without its number, which the next page then cites as equation (9). No density figure: 1,905 words on those pages against 614 claimed, with three other spans overlapping them.

note: Thirty-sixth type-A record and the fourth instruction-template naming in a row, the smallest of the four at five moves crossed with three forms. Each body is one fixed sentence around a slot, so only the slot names anything, and the five slots are the subsection's own moves: logistic family selection, uncertainty-aware parameter claim, time-to-state derivative conversion, environment-ready growth interface, finite-rate slowdown explanation. The artifact's chapter span is wrong and the record is coded from the pages: it allots model-establishment one physical page, file 7, with 139 words and five paragraphs, but the table of contents puts 3.1 on printed 4 and 3.2 on printed 6, so the section runs from the bottom of printed page 4 to the top of printed page 6, and the one page it does claim also carries the start of 3.2 and 3.3, so the 139 words are the subsection's move labels and not its prose. Span coded is section 3.1 entire, file pages 5 to 7: the goal and the problem quote, Table 1, the maximal-growth assumption, the wingspan-to-height conversion, the cube law m = a h cubed with a = 0.01134408, Balerion picked from lore, Figure 2 with Aegon at 6 ft 4 in, the 10:1 length to height ratio and 76 m, the length-cube ratio to 6,000,000 kg, the observation that a hundred years changed nothing so growth must slow, the choice of a sigmoidal curve, (1), the chi-squared fit with L = 843.717523 and k = 0.71173635, the derivative, and the change of variables to (2). Two things are right and I checked each: (2) is the exact derivative of m = a h cubed through the logistic, 3 m k (1 - (m / (a L cubed)) to the one third) with the 1/365 converting a per-year rate to a per-day one, so the algebra and the unit conversion both hold; and the wingspan-to-height factor is used consistently, 2520.5 over 3.75 giving 672 in at six years and 240 over 3.75 giving 64 in at eighteen months. Verified defects. The fitted pair (L, k) does not fit the data it is said to have been fitted to: with t0 solved from the birth point the curve gives 19.1 in at one year against a measured 16, 27.0 at eighteen months against 64 and 378.8 at six years against 672, and with t0 solved from the six-year point it gives 43.8 in at birth against 9.5, 84.6 at one year against 16 and 115.8 at eighteen months against 64; the best single t0 for the printed pair mispredicts birth by a factor of 3.5 and one year by a factor of 4.2. t0 itself is never printed anywhere in the paper, so (1) as written cannot be evaluated by a reader and every downstream number rests on a curve the paper does not specify. The chi-squared test the names call uncertainty-aware is never shown: no residuals, no statistic, no standard errors on L or k, and no statement of which of the four table points entered the fit. The cube law with a fitted at the hatchling explodes: 9.5 in gives 9.7 kg, matching the 10 kg in the table, but the same a gives 46.5 kg at the one-year height of 16 in against the table's 35, 2,974 kg at eighteen months and 3,442,525 kg at six years, so the calibration reproduces the birth mass alone and then puts a six-year-old dragon at three and a half thousand tonnes. The two length statements in the same paragraph cannot both hold: the 10:1 ratio applied to Drogon's own 672 in height gives 171 m, while the paper calls Drogon 61 m long, and the Balerion figure of 76 m is that same ratio applied to a 304 in height, so the rule that produces Balerion contradicts the length the paper gives for Drogon, and the 6,000,000 kg for Balerion is the length-cube ratio (76/61) cubed times Drogon's 3.44 million kg, which is 6.66 million, roughly right as a ratio but built on a mass three orders above any animal. The logistic asymptote, a L cubed, is 6.81 million kg, 13.6 percent above the 6.0 million the paper derives for Balerion, so even the curve's ceiling overshoots the largest dragon the paper sizes. No density figure: about 810 clean words on the span against 139 claimed, a factor of nearly six.

note: Thirty-seventh type-A record and the fifth instruction-template naming in a row, the second largest stored list of the five at fourteen moves crossed with three forms. Only the move names anything: method-to-stochastic-traits rationale, nested object architecture, normalized habitat-factor construction, agent-state initialization, stochastic climate generator, resource-acquisition state transition, resource-gated settlement transition, allometry-to-integer prey demand, suitability-and-den movement rule, health-and-environment cost table, mate-conditional reproduction rule, fallback reproduction rule, daily survival reward update, fullness-binned mass transition. This is the agent-based half of the 2019 problem; the paper runs a differential equation model for one region beside it, and the artifact files only the ABM under model-establishment. Span is file pages 5 to 8, printed 2 to 5, section 4.2 entire: the motivation for an ABM, the 45-ecoregion map, the Earth object and dragon placement, region dryness, land and ice fractions, Table 1, the prey calorie mechanics and the suitability index, dragon initialisation, the globe timestep, the seasonal temperature generator and its figure, then the dragon's five phases with Table 2 between them, and the daily reward and fullness transitions. Correct and checked: the temperature generator is internally consistent, since 4S - 4(4 - C) is the same as 4(S - 4 + C) that the text names, and with S at its maximum of 4 and C at 2 the two draws give at most 16 + 2 times 4 times 4.25, exactly the 50 C ceiling the paragraph claims, reached in the tropical summer as stated; and the predation law's unit chain holds, a per-year energy law divided by 365 and then by 5000 kcal per prey unit, with the ceiling function making the answer an integer count of prey items, which is what the calorie rating 0 to 10 requires. Verified defects. Table 1 sets the arctic temperature to 0 and the suitability index divides the temperature by T, the maximum possible temperature of the region, so every arctic region carries a division by zero and its suitability is undefined or infinite, which is the opposite of the paper's own conclusion that the arctic is the hostile case. Two temperature encodings sit two pages apart: Table 1 puts the tropics at 15 C and temperate at 5, while the generator maps climate to 0, 1 and 2 and returns anything between minus 8 and 50 for the tropics, so a tropical winter is colder than the temperate mean the table gives. Table 2 and the hunting paragraph disagree on what a kill costs the region, 10 forests per activity in the table and one forest per prey in the text, a factor of ten over the same event. The forest level is written as (land - ice) over (1 + dryness) with no maximum, and the suitability index divides it by F, so the normalisers are never stated; the index is also called a weighted sum while every weight in the printed mean is one fifth. The predation law never prints a or b, so the paper's central energetics cannot be evaluated from the text, and the ceiling makes one prey item of up to 5000 kcal the minimum daily intake for any dragon of any mass, up to fifty times a hatchling's need. Gold mining draws a uniform count of twenty centred on current health, so a healthy dragon mines about a hundred nuggets a day against a maximum regional stock of 500, which empties any region's gold in five days and makes the 50-nugget den threshold trivial; the mining rate is capped by the stock but never by work. And reproduction at 25 percent a day with fecundity borrowed from clutch-laying reptiles gives each mature dragon about ninety offspring a year while the paper argues the opposite way round, lowering clutch size and raising frequency without checking the product. Density figure is honest here: 1,833 raw words on the span against 1,804 claimed, so the artifact counted table cells and formula fragments but lost almost nothing.

note: Thirty-eighth type-A record, the sixth instruction-template naming in a row and the first of the 2020 problem, ten moves crossed with three forms, thirty stored names for seventeen located blocks. Only the move names anything: space-time field definition, per-grid differenced autoregression, expected-difference recursion, normal-error uncertainty premise, lag-design matrix estimation, normal-equation solution, six-fold RMSE comparison, per-cell coefficient implementation, recursive residual-field forecast, deterministic-versus-ensemble branch. Span is file pages 8 to 10, printed 5 to 7: the opening claim that temperature is driven by radiation, heat loss and biological exchange so a vector autoregression is wanted, 4.1 the longitude-latitude field, the 690 fishing points with sixty years each, the sixty-year spring plot, the choice of ARIMA(p, d, 0), (2) the differenced autoregression, the normal residual, (3) the recursive expectation, the normality premise, (4) the prediction with its innovation, the fifty-year spread argument, 4.3.1 the design matrix (5), the normal equations (6), the k-fold search, the RMSE grid and ARIMA(1, 1, 0), and 4.3.2's handoff to the predicted field. Correct and checked: (6) is the ordinary least-squares solution to the system in (5), and (3) is the exact recursive expectation of (2), so estimator and prediction recursion both follow. The lag choice is also internally consistent, a model with one lag and one difference being written ARIMA(1, 1, 0). Verified defects. The printed design matrix runs off its own sample: the last row's target is the difference at p plus sixty, which for any positive order is past the sixty observations the paragraph above says exist, where the last target available is the difference at sixty. The four symbols are the same letter: the innovation is epsilon, its variance is written epsilon squared at the same index, the predictive variance is sigma squared with no relation to either, and the difference order d multiplies the notation inconsistently, (2) and (3) carrying the d-th difference while (4) carries the first. (4) is only valid for a first difference, though the model is fitted over a grid that includes other orders, and it adds a draw of the innovation to the prediction, so the printed forecast is a random realisation and not a forecast. The model cannot produce the warming the paper goes on to predict: with the autoregressive coefficient inside the unit circle the recursive expectation (3) decays to zero, so the expected fifty-year field is the present field and only the added noise moves, which means any predicted migration comes from the ensemble draws rather than from the fitted dynamics, and the fitted dynamics were chosen after finding no trend in the data. The data are spring temperature only, as Figure 5's caption says, while the model is stated for the temperature of the point with no season subscript, so the paper's fifty-year field silently inherits one season. No density figure: 754 raw words on the span against 1,005 claimed, an overcount of a third, the mirror image of the previous paper's near-exact count.

note: Thirty-ninth type-A record, the seventh instruction-template naming in a row, ten moves crossed with three forms, thirty stored names for twenty-two located blocks. Only the move names anything: reference-sequence definition, comparison-sequence definition, grey relational coefficient, relation-grade aggregation, original-to-AGO state, whitened differential equation, least-squares parameter interface, time-response solution, inverse accumulation recovery, posterior error-ratio validation. Span is file pages 6 to 8, printed 5 to 7: 4.2.1 grey relational analysis with the reference and comparison sequences, the coefficient and its two-level minima, Table 2, then 4.2.2 the case for a grey system, the choice of GM(1, 1) said to be enhanced with the influencing factors, the original sequence for 1980 to 2020, the whitened equation, the least-squares pair, the mean-generating operator, the exponential time response, the inverse accumulation, the residual definition and the two variances, then 4.2.3 with 225 locations, Figure 2, Table 3 and the acceptance sentence. Correct and checked: the relational coefficient is the standard form with the two-level minimum, the two-level maximum and the resolution constant; the whitened equation, the design matrix with the mean-generated regressor and a unit column, the least-squares pair, the exponential time response and the inverse accumulation are all the textbook GM(1, 1) and are written correctly; and every residual in Table 3 is the printed actual minus the printed prediction to the fourth decimal, all eight of them. Verified defects. The paper's central acceptance claim is false on its own table: the c ratio, the dispersion of the residuals over the dispersion of the observations, computed from the eight printed rows, is 4.0 on standard deviations and 16.0 on variances, against the grey-model thresholds of 0.35 for excellent, 0.5 for good and 0.65 for qualified, so the model is rejected by its own test while the text calls the ratio small and calls the model acceptable. The residuals say the same thing one way: every one after 2005 is negative and they grow monotonically to minus 1.44, the prediction rises 0.236 degrees a year while the observations rise 0.0013, and the mean residual is minus 0.556, which is bias and not dispersion, so a dispersion criterion cannot see it. The announced enhancement never appears: GM(1, 1) is introduced as enhanced with the other influencing factors, the correlation table ranks greenhouse gas, forest cover and population, and none of the three enters the differential equation, the design matrix or the response. Table 2 also cannot be produced by its own sub-values: the human grade is printed as 0.9988 above sub-factors of 0.9784 and 0.9132, the environmental grade as 0.6423 above 0.9388, and no grouping of 0.9784, 0.9388 and 0.9132 gives either number, the mean of all three being 0.9435. Two different target series are used in one section for the same quantity, twenty years of SST for the correlation and forty-one years from 1980 for the grey model, and the relational coefficient is written as a function of k on the left and of t on the right. The forecast has no bound: a grey model with a negative development coefficient grows without limit, and the paper extrapolates to 2070 from a sequence whose own validation point already overshoots by 1.4 degrees. No density figure: 854 raw words on the span against 985 claimed, an overcount of thirteen percent.

The snapshot count is wrong: the paper says m = 468, its own split is 446 training plus 12 testing, which is 458, and its own date range, December 1981 to January 2020 monthly, is 458 months, and the validation dates confirm 458, since snapshot 447 lands on February 2019 only if the first snapshot is December 1981, so 468 contradicts three other statements and the covariance's m minus one denominator is wrong by ten. The thermal bands come from the mean temperature of the catch, which is a catch-weighted average of where fish were taken and not a tolerance range, so a niche is read out of a distributional statistic and the location forecast becomes a level set of the temperature field, inheriting every error of the field. No density figure: 2,221 raw words on the span against 1,570 claimed.

Equation (1) multiplies a speed by a radius: the paper's own notation table defines the extension rate as a rate, and the equation sets the radius derivative equal to it times the radius, which carries millimetres squared per day against millimetres per day, so at three millimetres a day and a ten millimetre radius the right side is thirty times the length the left side measures. That error then travels through everything: the closed form (6) is algebraically correct for the equation printed above it, which is what makes the slip the only place the speed enters, and the block height in (3) is a ratio of radius to maximum radius divided by a parameter that is a speed. Equation (8) is a ratio of two quantities the notation table declares scaled to [0,1], so it has no upper bound: a species ranked 0.1 against a competitor ranked 1.0 contributes a coefficient of ten, and the product of that with a competitor occupying half the maximum radius is five, which drives the bracket of (7) negative and turns growth into shrinkage, with three such competitors multiplying it again. The two empirical laws are stacked multiplicatively: Figure 4 says the log of decomposition is linear in moisture tolerance, which makes decomposition a function of tolerance alone, while (11) multiplies that exponential by the growth rate, so a species that is both fast and broad suffers the penalty twice and neither figure's fit can be recovered from the model unless the growth rate is constant across species, which Figure 3 denies. And equation (5) reprints equations (3) and (4) together as a numbered display, so one of the eleven numbered equations carries no content.

The compare block is the paper's best single move and worth recording: it maps the problem onto scheduling n activities that each need Y+1 ordered jobs on Y+1 distinct machines, then says why the standard answers fail - parallel machines are identical, a sequence of jobs needs ordered precedence, and queueing theory assumes a queue can hold more than one, whereas here one occupant per site per night makes every arrival beyond the first balk with probability one. Three programs share the chapter and none is derived in full: a drone-and-repeater purchase program whose capability term is a scan-area denominator and whose cost term is a per-unit sum, a ten-year demand forecast that imports an untranslated commensurable-cycles method and only substitutes numbers into it, and a siting program that imports the Stanford path-loss model and reduces it once. The prose reads as a specification: every subsection opens with a route block naming what the next display is for, and the eleven figure and table blocks are all pointed at by a sentence that says what the reader should take from them. The span opens inside the assumption list, so two assumption bullets are counted as limit, and it includes the notation table and 2.4 data preprocessing, which fixes the twenty-kilometre repeater range that Task 3 later contradicts. Stored field is the densest measured in B and misplaced at both ends: 440 units in the paper, 152 on these sixteen pages, ten distinct function strings, 152 excerpts, one per 37 words, on pages 4 to 11 and 17 to 19 only. Files 12 to 16 carry no model-establishment unit at all, and those pages hold the greedy multiplexing algorithm, the weighted objective and its Pareto front, and the whole ternary commensurable prediction model; there the units are tagged algorithm, 60, and model-improvement, 30, so the paper's three most distinctive moves sit outside its own record. note: Section 4.2 to 4.4, 'Analysis', 'Construction' and 'Result' of the double-dam system, on printed 7 to 9: fifteen preserved blocks over 1,073 words of page text including the flow-diagram labels, seventy-two words a block, 3.6 times the live type median of 20, against a layout that claims 10 paragraphs and 1,202 words for 42 sentences. Four route, four define, three compute, one mechanism, one limit, one derive and one interpret, with source, select, read-figure, compare, check and handoff absent. This is the third Colorado River chapter in the pass and the only one written as a difference equation: papers 115 and 121 both model the reservoirs as volumes with fixed geometry, while this one never gives the lakes a shape at all and works directly on daily increments of stored water, which is why its block count is low and its word count per block is the highest in the B sample so far, above the sixty-four of the 2013 model chapter. The chapter's spine is a three-part announcement - analysis, construction, result - and the construction is three moves: abstract the two dams into two nodes with a one-directional arrow, write the daily increment of each node as an outflow-coefficient equation with an upstream inflow term, then solve the pair in closed form and hand the closed forms to a two-objective program whose objectives are the absolute gaps between demand and the water drawn at each dam. The interpret block is the only place in the span that argues, and it argues the right thing: the objectives are written as absolute differences because water drawn and not used is a loss, and the constraint that the extraction coefficients sum to less than one is there to keep the draw inside the stores. Span defects: the window opens in the middle of 4.1 with the formula that sums the demands and its result 0.54, so the chapter begins with the tail of a calculation it does not set up, and it closes inside 4.4 at 'about 2 trillion m3 within 61 days', so the result section arrives at the end of the model chapter rather than in a bucket of its own. The overlap is worse than one span: printed 8 is claimed by three buckets, `data-preprocessing` at 6 to 8, `problem-analysis` at 8 to 12 and this one at 8 to 10, and printed 10 is claimed by this one and by `results` at 10 to 17, so neither end of the span sits on a printed boundary and the window starts and stops inside two different sections. Arithmetic defects a reader can run: the paragraph announces that four demands are added and the formula sums five terms, k from 1 to 5; the summed demand is printed as 0.54 with no unit while every later quantity in the span is in millions or billions of cubic metres, and the demand used downstream is never reconciled with it; and 40.7 million cubic metres a day for 61 days is 2.48 billion, not the 'about 2 trillion' the same sentence prints, a factor of a thousand. Figures 5 and 6 are named as the basis of the model and neither is read back: the six outflow coefficients that Figure 6 labels are defined in prose instead. Stored field: 30 units on these three pages, 2 on printed 7, 15 on printed 8 and 13 on printed 9, with 30 distinct excerpts and 9 distinct function strings - a sentence-level field again, and its weight follows the algebra rather than the argument, since printed 9, which carries the closed forms and the program, supplies six of the fifteen blocks and thirteen of the thirty units while printed 7 supplies two units.

note: Section 3, 'Model Design', on printed 8 to 16: thirty-six preserved blocks over 2,875 words of page text, eighty words a block, 3.9 times the live 20.5-block median, against a layout that claims 33 paragraphs and 3,172 words for 174 sentences. Thirteen define, seven limit, four derive, three route, three source, two mechanism, one each read-figure, select, compute and interpret, with compare, check and handoff absent. The seven limits are the finding: a B chapter usually carries three percent limit blocks, and this one carries nineteen, because its every subsection runs the same three-part header - modelling ideas, then supplementary assumptions and justifications, then calculations - so each of the four sections states its assumptions as labelled bullets with a paragraph of justification under each, and the assumption becomes a block rather than a clause. That header is the most transferable thing in the chapter. Wildlife sets up two measures and one normalization; natural resources sets up grass and water; financial interest sets up four revenue streams and one sigmoid; animal tourism sets up an encounter probability and two impact factors; and each closes on one score in [0,1]. The four scores then pass through a pairwise-weight step per land type - wildlife preservation zone, human settlement zone, grazing zone - and into a weighted total, so the chapter's whole argument is that a multi-objective evaluation is assembled from four separately normalized subscores and one consistency-checked weight vector. Verified arithmetic: the three comparison matrices are reciprocal in all eighteen printed entries, and the consistency ratios reproduce from the printed matrices to three decimals - geometric-mean weights give CR 0.0608, 0.0224 and 0.0300 against the printed 0.0612, 0.0223 and 0.0301, and RI = 0.90 is the right index for n = 4 - so this is the rare B chapter whose weight step a reader can rerun. Nine policies and eight scenarios per land type also reconcile with the announced twenty-four. What cannot be rerun is everything the scores consume. The livestock regression, the local-population regression and the tourist-population regression are printed only as Figures 3 and 5, with no coefficient, no error term and no interval, so the stock density, three of the four revenue streams and the encounter rate are all unreachable from the page; the white noise added to the livestock fit is described as normal and never given a variance. The grass equation prints b = 1/4000 ha/kg while its own annotation calls 1/b the ceiling yield in kgDM/ha, so the sigmoid's V/b divides a mass per area by an area per mass and the term is not dimensionless, and the factor of 4 in front of the growth term appears in no sentence. The water-stress scale defined on printed 12 - four states, levels 0 to 3 - is never used: the score that follows is a weighted sum of the four state frequencies, 0.6, 0.3, 0.1 and 0, so the level definition is dead on arrival. The third score's 15000 USD constant is called 'derived from normalization' and nothing else. The span ends mid-sentence on printed 16, 'providing a forum for bring together', inside 3.2's policy explanation, so the scenario results the introduction promised sit outside the stored chapter entirely. Figure 4 is the only figure read; Figures 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 are pointed at in a clause.

Derive at forty-two percent against the type's nine is the finding: this is the textbook shape, a chapter that writes ten numbered equations with their symbols and almost nothing else, where the 2023 paper coded before it on the same problem writes thirty-six blocks of definitions and four equations. Same problem, same year, opposite chapter. The spine is worth copying even so: two benefit streams are announced, each is built from a normalised index, the reserve is discretised into 36 grids of 50 square kilometres, each grid gets four binary land uses, and the constraints then close the model in four moves - exclusivity, precedence of protection, a threshold map from ecological value to land use, and a visitor cap. Exclusivity (5) and precedence (6) are internally sound: the four binaries sum to one in every region, and the protected count is required to beat each alternative. The visitor cap checks as well: 150,000 visitors a year is the 411 the text rounds to 410, and forty people per tourist area times the eight, nine and ten tourist areas the solver returns stays at or under it. The threshold map is where the chapter breaks. The prose sets three bands, above 0.5 for protection, 0.4 to 0.5 for tourism, below 0.2 for agriculture, and never explains the 0.2-to-0.4 band at all; the equations set four, and they put hunting in the band the prose gives to tourism, so (8) forbids Z in exactly the interval the sentence before it says is suitable for tourists. The lowest band (10) then allows every combination including X alone, so the region the prose sends to agriculture may come back as pure protection. The ecological score does not normalise at all: the species weights, lions 1, elephants 0.8, zebras 0.5, antelopes minus 0.3, giraffes 0.4, run outside [0,1] by construction, so (3) cannot return the index the section promises, and the negative weight makes an abundant prey species count as damage. Checked on the render, (4) adds the plant term rather than subtracting it, Vx = B1 Ax + B2 Px, but the next page assumes vegetation cover is equal in every region, so B2 Px is a constant shift and the ranking of regions by ecological value is B1 Ax alone; (2), which exists to normalise that cover, then decides nothing. Eight mechanism, four derive, four interpret, three limit, three source, two route, with read-figure, compare, check and handoff absent. Mechanism at a third of the blocks against the type's four percent is the finding, and it is the opposite of paper 126: where that chapter writes an equation and leaves it, this one writes an equation and then spends two or three blocks saying what each term is for - the poaching term as a Gordon-Schaefer harvest, the migration pair, the predator's two losses, the logistic baseline, the tourism regulator, the seasonal cycle. The verbal floor under every symbol is what makes the chapter readable and what makes it long. The spine is six ordinary differential equations announced as a partition before any of them is written - two for fauna, two for the human macroscope, two for the local effects - then Lotka-Volterra with the extra terms nailed on one at a time, then a final section that reassembles them and only then numbers them. That announce, extend, reassemble order is the copyable shape, and the assumptions are written as a labelled list, E-1 to RK-3, each tied to the term it licenses. Verified against the page: the parameter census is exact, Table 1's rows giving 7, 4, 2, 5, 6 and 2 parameters for the six equations, twenty-six in all, which is the same twenty-six section 6 announces, with six starting conditions in Table 3 and those values consistent with the prose of 6.1 - 34 hundred-thousand prey as low millions, 4 thousand predators as a few thousand, 3 hundred-thousand visits as the 300,000 annual visitors. Read on the render, (5.2) and (5.1) match their prose term for term, including the boma term and the two migration terms, and (5.3)'s minus sign on degradation is the one the text claims. What the chapter states and does not implement is the defect family here. P-1 says the change in poaching is regulated by a delay of information factor, and (5.5) has no delay in it: gamma multiplies an instantaneous bracket, so the announced lag never enters the model. E-3 and P-3 do enter as I_0 and lambda_0. The two migration terms m_0 and m are the only terms in (5.1) that no assumption in 3.4 to 3.6 licenses. This is the fourth shape in the 2024 B papers and the plainest: one chapter that builds a second-order vertical equation of motion out of Newton's second law and stops at Runge-Kutta. The drag term is squared, so it keeps one sign whatever the direction of travel, while the prose under (4) promises that the resistance is always opposite to the movement; a descent therefore receives a downward drag. Its rho(z) is depth-dependent while (3) prints the correction as the literal factor 1.022 - 0.01z/1500 tagged g/cm^3, a density in grams per cubic centimetre multiplying gV against a notation table that gives rho in kg/m^3. And the sentence above it says the equation is obtained from equations (2), (3), (4), (5) and (6), citing (6) as one of its own inputs. The same chapter also contradicts itself in three places a reader can check without a calculator. Section 5.1 opens by asserting that the submersible, on losing contact, immediately ceases movement and ascends promptly whether or not it still has propulsion, and the safety strategy on page 5 argued for staying put; two blocks later the same section says that if the other power systems fail it cannot expel ballast and may sink to the seabed or hover at a neutral-buoyancy point, with the tank mass fixed at its initial value. The extractor counts 4,160 words on those five pages, of which 2,750 are watermark glyphs on four of the five, leaving about 1,410 words of prose, forty-seven a block, 1.4 times the 21-block median. The shape is three parallel accounts summed the same way. Section 3.2 builds a tourist count and a profit; 3.3 builds an environmental level from a carbon term, a resilience index and a logistic investment return; 3.4 builds the same for the social side with a second logistic. Each of the three ends in one aggregate - P, E and S - each is a sum over the same 365 days, and each borrows its saturating term from the same logistic. The transferable idea is the unit conversion: the chapter states that the contingent valuation method lets every non-monetary indicator be read as money, and only after that claims the three may be added, which is the one honest sentence about aggregating heterogeneous terms in the whole B sample. What the chapter does not do is optimize: the stored opening announces a multi-objective nonlinear program with PSO and the constraints E <= E0 and S <= S0, and the span then builds E and S and stops, with no program, no objective and no constraint in it. Four things in it are arithmetic a reader can run. The carbon constant is off by a factor of a thousand: the prose gives 66.13 kg of carbon a tourist a day and 190 dollars a tonne, and the next display prints Delta E1 = 12564.7 sum N(t), which is exactly 66.13 times 190, kilograms multiplied by a per-tonne price; in tonnes the cost is 12.56 dollars a tourist a day. The seasons are defined as t = 1 to 120 and 271 to 365 off-peak against 121 to 270 peak, and the second constraint then sums t = 1 to 120 and t = 211 to 366, sixty days that belong to the peak season plus a day 366 that does not exist, while the peak constraint sums 121 to 270 and integrates 121 to 220. With those printed bounds the solution the paper reports, A = 16822 and B = 5514, returns 1,985,648 for the first constraint against the printed 1,669,500 and 1,244,543 for the second against 398,000; solving the printed pair gives A = 34,742 and B = -13,171, so the only root violates the model's own condition that A and B be positive. Against the season definition the printed pair gives 407,948 for the second constraint, 2.5 percent high, so that one is a range slip rather than a fit. And the aggregate E sums its investment term inside the sum over t, so a quantity that does not depend on time is added 365 times; S divides the same term by 365, showing that the authors saw the problem in one display and not in the other. Three more do not resolve. The policy adjustment sets N(t) = min{N0(t), c1} in the peak season and max{N0(t), c2} off it, with c1 and c2 given no value anywhere in the span, and the off-peak branch raises the count to c2 although the cosine was defined with a max against zero for exactly the reason that winter numbers are negligible. The resilience index is written ERI = sum 1/(1 + beta N(t)) ERI_max, a sum of 365 dimensionless fractions, and E2 is then described as the yearly sum of ERI, a sum of a sum, with beta never quantified. And the social weight is fixed by setting sigma2 = 1 'for the sake of convenience', which makes sigma1 = 2.155 - from (31% + 46% x 38%) / (11% + 46% x 25%), arithmetic that does check - mean that one dimension out of the three is weighted more than twice the others by assumption rather than by argument.
